Research/MDOC
Feasible generation

MDOC
Generate feasible motion. Coordinate safely.

A useful motion plan must obey the robot's dynamics and avoid collisions, even when many robots share the same space. MDOC brings these requirements inside model-based diffusion: candidate controls are corrected during rollout, and known dynamics turn them into executable state trajectories. The planner estimates its denoising direction from evaluated rollouts without learning from demonstrations. MDOC-CBS then uses the same low-level mechanism to resolve conflicts between robots.

Read the paperFigures & tablesRun this methodOriginal code

The question

Can we generate dynamically feasible, collision-free motion without demonstration training, and use that planner to coordinate a team of robots?

Demonstrations

How it works

01

Let the model guide generation

Instead of querying a learned score network, MDOC samples control sequences, rolls them through known dynamics, and evaluates their costs. Monte Carlo Score Ascent estimates a direction that progressively refines the trajectory distribution toward useful solutions.

02

Correct controls inside the rollout

A Control Barrier Function defines local safety conditions. At each rollout step, MDOC projects a proposed control onto the corresponding constraint half-spaces before advancing the dynamics. Safety correction therefore acts on the inputs that generate the motion.

03

Coordinate through conflict resolution

MDOC-CBS separates individual planning from team coordination. Conflict-Based Search identifies inter-robot collisions and adds constraints; affected robots replan with MDOC. The same projection mechanism handles obstacle and inter-robot constraints.

Results

Paper results compare MDOC with single-robot planners and evaluate MDOC-CBS on multi-robot coordination and larger maps.

Multi-robot scale
Up to 40 robots

Reported on larger maps, including the 6 × 6 benchmark; the standard 2 × 2 experiments evaluate up to 20 robots.

Planning-time reduction
5–10×

Relative to MMD-CBS in the reported 2 × 2 Empty and Conveyor experiments, at comparable conflict-tree expansion levels.

Scope & trade-offs

Training-free single-robot motion planning and CBS-based multi-robot coordination in simulated continuous environments with known dynamics. The main experiments use a single-integrator model, with additional dynamics studies in the appendix.

Success is not universal: tight random maps expose Monte Carlo variance and a trade-off between exploration and aggressive CBF correction.

The paper's demonstrated multi-robot scale depends on map, horizon, dynamics, and computational budget; it is not a general deployment guarantee.

Online receding-horizon use, richer dynamics, and improved projection efficiency are identified as future directions.

The next question

In tightly constrained environments, aggressive safety correction can restrict exploration and increase rollout variability. MD-COAS takes up this question: how can soft feasibility guidance and hard correction work together throughout denoising?
